title: Typeahead System Design: How Google Autocomplete Works (2026)
description: Learn typeahead system design step by step: tries, precomputed top-k suggestions, sharding, and caching to serve autocomplete in under 100ms. Master it here.
content:
Typeahead System Design: Why Google Autocomplete Is a Favorite Interview Question

You type "how to" into Google, and before your finger leaves the keyboard, ten suggestions appear. That feature is called typeahead (or autocomplete), and "Design Google Typeahead" is one of the most common system design interview questions. It looks simple on the surface, but it forces you to combine a classic data structure, an offline data pipeline, sharding, and aggressive caching into one coherent design.

What Makes Typeahead So Hard? The 100ms Budget

Here is the constraint that shapes the entire design: every single keystroke is a request. If a user types "cricket score", that is not one request. That is thirteen requests, one per character.

An average user types a character every 200 to 300 milliseconds. Your suggestion must appear before the next keystroke lands, or it is useless. Subtract network travel time, and your server has a latency budget of under 100 milliseconds, often closer to 20 or 30 milliseconds of actual computation.

Compare that with a normal search: users will tolerate a full second for search results. They will not tolerate suggestions that lag behind their typing. If you are new to thinking in milliseconds, start with my guide on latency and how it is measured, because this whole design is an exercise in cutting latency.

One more number to say out loud in the interview: if Google handles billions of searches per day, and each search generates 10 to 15 keystroke requests, the typeahead service receives an order of magnitude more traffic than search itself. Huge traffic plus a tiny latency budget. That is the problem.

The Chai Stall Analogy: Precompute, Don't Compute

Near my old office there was a chai stall. The owner knew his regulars. The moment he saw me park my bike, he started making my usual order. By the time I reached the counter, the chai was ready. He did not take my order and then start working. He predicted the order and prepared it in advance.

That is the core insight of typeahead system design. With 30 milliseconds of budget, you cannot run a database query, rank millions of matching phrases, and sort them at request time. The winning move is the chai stall move: do the expensive work ahead of time, and at request time just hand over what is already prepared.

Everything that follows, the trie, the precomputed top-k lists, the offline pipeline, is just this one idea applied carefully.

How Does a Trie Power Prefix Matching?

The natural data structure for autocomplete is the trie (prefix tree). A trie stores strings character by character: the root is empty, each edge adds one character, and every path from the root spells a prefix.

Why not a database with a LIKE 'cri%' query? Because scanning millions of rows per keystroke will blow the latency budget instantly. A trie gives you all phrases sharing a prefix by walking one path.

Step-by-Step: Serving the Prefix "cri"

  1. The user has typed "cri". The request arrives at the suggestion service.
  2. Start at the root of the trie. Follow the edge for c, then r, then i. That is exactly three hops, one per character.
  3. You are now at the node representing "cri". Every phrase in the subtree below it ("cricket", "cricket score", "crime news") is a valid completion.
  4. Return the best few phrases from that subtree to the user.

Reaching the node costs O(L), where L is the length of the prefix, and L is tiny. The trap is step 4. If the subtree under "cri" holds 500,000 phrases, you cannot rank them per request. This is where precomputation enters.

Precomputing Top-K Suggestions vs Computing on the Fly

Option 1: Compute on the Fly

Walk to the prefix node, traverse the whole subtree, look up each phrase's popularity, sort, and return the top 10. This is correct and always fresh, but for short prefixes like "a" or "th" the subtree is enormous. Traversal alone can take hundreds of milliseconds. The budget is gone.

Option 2: Precompute Top-K at Every Node

Instead, store the answer directly on the node. Each trie node keeps its own top-k list (usually k = 5 or 10): the k most popular full phrases that start with that prefix, already ranked.

Now a request is: walk L characters, read a precomputed list, return it. A few memory lookups. Single-digit milliseconds.

The trade-offs, which you should state explicitly in an interview:

  • Storage cost: every node duplicates up to k phrases (or pointers to them). You pay memory to buy speed. For typeahead, that trade is obviously worth it.
  • Update cost: when a phrase gets more popular, the top-k lists of all its prefix nodes may need updating. So you do not update the trie on the hot path at all, which leads to the offline pipeline.

Where Do Suggestions Come From? The Offline Aggregation Pipeline

The trie has to be built from something. The source is the query log: a record of what people actually search for.

Sampling: You Do Not Need Every Log Entry

At Google scale, logging and processing every single query is expensive and unnecessary. If "cricket score" is searched millions of times a day, recording one out of every thousand occurrences still measures its popularity accurately. Popular queries stay popular in a sample. So the pipeline samples the logs, which cuts processing cost by orders of magnitude at almost no accuracy loss.

The Pipeline, End to End

  1. Collect: search services write sampled queries to a log store.
  2. Aggregate: a periodic batch job (MapReduce or Spark style) groups identical queries and counts frequencies over a time window, for example the last 7 days.
  3. Rank and filter: compute a popularity score per phrase, and drop spam, offensive phrases, and one-off junk queries.
  4. Build: construct a fresh trie with top-k lists baked into every node.
  5. Ship: push the new trie to the serving fleet and atomically swap it in. Old trie serves traffic until the moment the new one takes over.

Notice the clean separation: the serving path is read-only and blazing fast, while all writes happen offline where latency does not matter. If the interviewer asks "how fresh are the suggestions?", the honest answer is "as fresh as the last pipeline run", maybe hourly or daily, and for pure typeahead that staleness is acceptable. Trending topics need a separate fast path, covered below.

How Do You Shard the Prefix Space?

A trie for billions of phrases will not fit on one machine, and one machine cannot serve the traffic anyway. So you shard by prefix: different servers own different regions of the prefix space.

The naive scheme, one shard per starting letter (server 1 gets "a", server 2 gets "b"), fails because the alphabet is not uniform. Vastly more queries start with "s" or "t" than with "x" or "z". The "s" server melts while the "x" server sleeps.

The better scheme is to shard by load, not by letter. Analyze historical traffic and cut the prefix space into ranges with roughly equal query volume: one hot prefix range like "s" through "sm" might be a shard by itself, while "u" through "z" together form another. A small lookup service maps an incoming prefix to the shard that owns it. This is the same balancing problem you meet when partitioning any keyspace, and the standard tool for it is covered in my consistent hashing guide.

Each shard is then replicated, because the data is read-only between pipeline runs. Replicas of a hot shard multiply its throughput and give you fault tolerance for free.

Caching at Every Layer: Browser, CDN, Server

Typeahead traffic has a beautiful property: it is extremely repetitive. Millions of people type the same popular prefixes every hour, and the answers barely change between pipeline runs. That makes it a dream workload for caching.

  • Browser cache: if the user types "cric", deletes a character, and retypes it, the browser should reuse the earlier response instead of calling the server again. A short TTL (say, one hour) on suggestion responses eliminates a chunk of traffic before it leaves the device.
  • CDN / edge cache: responses for popular prefixes can be cached at edge servers close to users. The head of the distribution, the few thousand hottest prefixes, covers a huge share of all requests, so a small edge cache absorbs enormous load.
  • Server-side cache: in front of the trie shards, an in-memory cache (Redis style) holds recently requested prefix results, shielding the shards from repeated work.

Each layer cuts both latency and backend load. If the layering of these caches is new to you, my post on caching strategies walks through the patterns in detail.

One practical client-side trick worth mentioning: debouncing. For very fast typists, the client can wait 30 to 50 milliseconds after a keystroke before firing the request, so intermediate prefixes that the user blows past never generate traffic at all.

Want to master this with video lessons and real case studies? This topic is covered in depth in my Udemy course System Design Fundamentals for Interviews — 5.5 hours, rated 4.8★, built from real interview questions.

Filtering the Results: Personalization and Trending

A single global top-k list is a good baseline, but real systems layer two refinements on top.

Personalization

Two users typing "j" should not see identical suggestions. A cricket fan might see "jasprit bumrah" while a developer sees "java download". The serving layer fetches the global top-k from the trie, then re-ranks a small candidate set using the user's search history, language, and location. Because re-ranking touches only 10 to 20 candidates, it stays cheap. This is the same "generate candidates, then rank them" pattern used in the Facebook News Feed design.

Trending Queries

The offline pipeline is hours behind reality. When breaking news happens, people expect the related suggestion within minutes. So you run a small real-time stream alongside the batch pipeline: it watches the live query stream for sudden spikes, keeps a short list of trending phrases with time-decayed scores, and the server merges that list into the trie's results at request time.

Safety Filtering

Finally, a filter layer removes offensive, harmful, or policy-violating phrases. Cheap to mention, expensive to forget: suggesting a harmful query is far worse than suggesting nothing, so this filter runs both offline (during trie build) and online (on the merged results).

How to Talk About Typeahead in an Interview

Here is a 30-second answer you can memorize and adapt:

"Typeahead is latency-critical: every keystroke is a request, and the answer must arrive in under 100 milliseconds, so nothing expensive can happen at request time. I'd build a trie over popular queries, and precompute the top 10 suggestions at every node so a request is just walking the prefix and reading a stored list. The trie is built offline by a batch pipeline that samples query logs, aggregates frequencies, and ships a fresh trie periodically. I'd shard the trie by prefix ranges balanced on load, replicate shards for read throughput, and cache aggressively at the browser, CDN, and server. On top of that, a lightweight layer re-ranks results for personalization and merges in trending queries from a real-time stream."

Then let the interviewer pick a thread. Common follow-ups and the one-line answers:

  • "Why not query a database per keystroke?" Latency. A scan-and-rank per keystroke cannot meet a sub-100ms budget at this traffic volume.
  • "What if a shard gets hot?" Split its prefix range, add replicas, and let the edge cache absorb the head of the distribution.
  • "How do new trending queries show up quickly?" A real-time spike detector on the query stream, merged with trie results at serve time.
  • "How much storage does top-k per node cost?" Roughly k references per node; you trade memory for guaranteed read speed, which is the right trade here.

Key Takeaways

  • Every keystroke is a request, so typeahead needs a sub-100ms budget and gets more traffic than search itself.
  • A trie with precomputed top-k lists per node turns each request into a short walk plus one read. Precompute, don't compute.
  • An offline pipeline samples query logs, aggregates frequencies, and periodically rebuilds and ships the trie, keeping the serving path read-only.
  • Shard the prefix space by load, not alphabetically, and replicate shards for throughput.
  • Cache at browser, CDN, and server layers, then layer personalization, trending, and safety filtering on top of the global results.

Next Steps

Typeahead pulls together almost everything in this series: latency budgets, precomputation, batch pipelines, sharding, and caching. If any of those felt shaky, browse the full System Design Tutorial series from the start, and make sure you are solid on consistent hashing, because balanced partitioning shows up in nearly every design question you will face next.
